z-m-38-01.title: As we widen the domain, how do the maximum and minimum move?
z-m-38-01.topic: Maximum and minimum of a quadratic function when the domain changes
z-m-38-01.goal: As the end k of the domain changes, check with value tables how the place where the maximum and minimum occur (the vertex or an endpoint) changes, and restate your first prediction.
z-m-38-01.material: Here is the quadratic function f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 (read as: 'x squared minus 4x plus 3'). Set the domain to 0 ≤ x ≤ k (k is a positive real number), change k, and look at the maximum and minimum of f on that domain. Seoyeon predicted: “If the interval gets wider, the minimum gets smaller and the maximum gets larger.” The value tables are revealed one at a time, step by step.
z-m-38-01.thinking.0: Test a prediction using value tables as evidence
z-m-38-01.thinking.1: Keep or revise your judgment as new information arrives
z-m-38-01.thinking.2: Say, using intervals, how the conclusion changes when the condition (the domain) changes
z-m-38-01.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty level assigned in production; it does not mean the curriculum places this content in high school grade 1. Assume the prerequisites below have already been learned.
z-m-38-01.prereq.1: Rewriting a quadratic function in the form y=a(x−p)²+q to find the vertex (completing the square)
z-m-38-01.prereq.2: The shape of the graph of a quadratic function and its axis of symmetry
z-m-38-01.prereq.3: Calculating function values yourself to make a value table
z-m-38-01.s.s1.prompt: The value tables are revealed one at a time. At each step, make a judgment from the data so far, and when the next data appears, keep or revise that judgment. (The domain is always 0 ≤ x ≤ k.)
z-m-38-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write down the pairs of x and f(x) from the revealed table, and mark where the smallest and largest values occur.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.hint.1: Rewrite f(x) in the form (x−□)²+□, and check whether the x where the smallest value occurs in that form lies inside the domain.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.info: This is the value table for k = 1 (0 ≤ x ≤ 1). When x = 0, f = 3; when x = 0.5, f = 1.25; when x = 1, f = 0. On this interval the minimum is 0 and the maximum is 3.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: If we keep increasing k beyond 1, what do you think will happen to the minimum? (Predict using only the tables and the formula so far.)
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.after: With only three tables, both a and b are possible predictions. If you thought of the shape of the formula (opens upward), b is natural; if you looked only at the trend of the values getting smaller, you get a. Let's test it with the next table.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: As k increases, the minimum keeps getting smaller
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You continued from only the trend of decreasing values. A quadratic function changes direction at some point, so you need to check whether that point lies inside the interval.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: From some k on, it may stop getting smaller
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This prediction comes from remembering that the graph opens upward, so it has a lowest point. Where that lowest point is has to be checked with the table.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: No matter what k is, the minimum stays 0
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You looked only at values inside the interval and did not think about values outside it. When the interval gets wider, new x values come in.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.info: This is the value table for k = 3 (0 ≤ x ≤ 3). When x = 1, f = 0; when x = 2, f = −1; when x = 3, f = 0. Also, when x = 2.5, f = −0.75. The minimum is −1.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: If we increase k further, to k = 5 or k = 10, what will happen to the minimum?
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Since f(x) = (x−2)² − 1, the lowest value −1 occurs at x = 2, and for x greater than 2 the values rise again. So whenever k is 2 or more, the minimum is the same, −1. If you chose a at first, point out which table changed your prediction.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You did not notice that the values rise again after passing x = 2. Compare the values just before and just after x = 2 in the table.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It does not change any more from −1
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This judgment reads from the table that the value is lowest at x = 2 and rises after that.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: From k = 3 on, the minimum actually gets larger
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: When the interval gets wider, the minimum can only get smaller or stay the same; it cannot get larger. You missed that all the values from the earlier interval are still included when the interval gets wider.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.info: For k = 4 (0 ≤ x ≤ 4): when x = 0, f = 3, and when x = 4, f = 3, so the two endpoints have the same value. The maximum is 3. When we widen to k = 5, f = 8 at x = 5 becomes the new maximum.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: How should Seoyeon's prediction “if the interval gets wider, the maximum gets larger” be corrected?
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.after: For 0 ≤ k ≤ 4, f(k) ≤ 3, so the maximum is f(0) = 3, and from k > 4 on, f(k) becomes greater than 3. Seoyeon's prediction is right only when k < 2 for the minimum, and only when k > 4 for the maximum. The range where it is right splits depending on the condition (the interval).
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: As soon as k increases, the maximum also increases, so Seoyeon is right as she said
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You did not check that the maximum stays at 3 when k = 3 and k = 4. You need to compare whether the newly added x values give something larger than the existing maximum.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: No matter how much k increases, the maximum stays at 3
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You missed that f(5) = 8 appears at k = 5. You need to check whether the value at the endpoint keeps growing.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Until k reaches 4 the maximum stays 3, and it grows only after k passes 4
z-m-38-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This judgment compares which of the two endpoints, x = 0 and x = k, has the larger value.
z-m-38-01.s.s1.reflect: Some people first predicted “the minimum keeps getting smaller” and changed their mind after seeing the table beyond x = 2, and others predicted “it may stop” and kept that prediction. In one line, say which table changed (or kept) your judgment.
z-m-38-01.s.s2.prompt: On the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ k, choose the k for which (maximum) − (minimum) = 4. (k is a positive real number.)
z-m-38-01.s.s2.hint.0: For k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, organize the maximum and minimum in a table and find the difference.
z-m-38-01.s.s2.hint.1: Mark the k values in the table where the difference is 4, and test whether it is the same for k in between (for example 2.5 and 3.5).
z-m-38-01.s.s2.o.a: The difference is 4 only when k = 4, and not for any other k
z-m-38-01.s.s2.r.a: You checked only that the difference is 4 at k = 4 and did not test the values next to it (for example 3.5).
z-m-38-01.s.s2.o.b: The difference is 4 only when k = 3, and not for any other k
z-m-38-01.s.s2.r.b: You checked only that it works at one value and did not test the values around it.
z-m-38-01.s.s2.o.c: The difference is 4 for every real number k that is 4 or more (all the way from k = 4)
z-m-38-01.s.s2.r.c: You did not check that at k = 5, the maximum is 8 and the minimum is −1, so the difference is 9.
z-m-38-01.s.s2.o.d: The difference is 4 for every real number k from 2 to 4
z-m-38-01.s.s2.r.d: This judgment found the range in which the minimum stays −1 and the maximum stays 3 on the interval.
z-m-38-01.s.s2.explain: For 2 ≤ k ≤ 4, the minimum is −1 (at x = 2) and the maximum is 3 (at x = 0), so the difference is 4. If k < 2, the minimum is greater than −1, so the difference is less than 4; if k > 4, the maximum f(k) is greater than 3, so the difference is greater than 4.

z-m-38-02.title: Is the graph determined just because two points have the same height?
z-m-38-02.topic: Determining the formula of a quadratic function, and whether the conditions are sufficient
z-m-38-02.goal: For the quadratic function f(x)=ax²+bx+c with f(0)=3 and f(4)=3, sort out what must be added for the formula to be determined uniquely, and for conditions that do not determine it, build several formulas that satisfy all the conditions.
z-m-38-02.material: For the quadratic function f(x) = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0; a, b, c are constants; read as: 'a x squared plus b x plus c'), two things are known. The graph passes through the point (0, 3) and the point (4, 3). That is, f(0) = 3 and f(4) = 3. This information alone does not determine the formula of f uniquely. We are going to give one more piece of information.
z-m-38-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
z-m-38-02.thinking.2: Building several formulas that satisfy the same conditions
z-m-38-02.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty level assigned in production; it does not mean the curriculum places this content in high school grade 1. Assume the prerequisites below have already been learned.
z-m-38-02.prereq.1: Substituting the coordinates of a point into the quadratic y=ax²+bx+c to form a relation among the coefficients
z-m-38-02.prereq.2: The fact that two points at the same height are symmetric about the axis of symmetry
z-m-38-02.prereq.3: The sign of the discriminant b²−4ac and the number of points where the graph meets the x-axis
z-m-38-02.s.s1.prompt: From the information below, choose all the pieces of information such that “adding just that one piece makes the formula of f uniquely determined.”
z-m-38-02.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one candidate piece of information and build two formulas that satisfy it together with f(0)=3 and f(4)=3. If you can build two, that information is not enough.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.hint.1: First write down what relation arises between the coefficients b and a when f(0)=3 and f(4)=3.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.r.a: It tells you only that a is positive, so there are still many possible values of a. If you try a = 1 and a = 2, both are possible.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.o.b: The minimum value of f is −1
z-m-38-02.s.s1.r.b: This choice recognizes that a minimum exists and that using its value together lets you find a.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.o.c: The graph meets the x-axis at two different points
z-m-38-02.s.s1.r.c: This is possible not only when a is positive but also when it is negative, and even for positive a, many values are possible. You did not test whether several values of a satisfy the condition.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.o.d: The graph passes through the point (1, 0)
z-m-38-02.s.s1.r.d: This choice recognizes that a new point adds one more new relation to the formula, which determines the coefficient.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.o.e: The graph passes through the point (4, 3)
z-m-38-02.s.s1.r.e: This just restates information that was already given, so it adds no new relation. You have to tell apart new information from information you already know.
z-m-38-02.s.s1.explain: If f(0)=3 and f(4)=3, the axis of symmetry is x = 2 and the formula has the form f(x)=a(x−2)²+k. If the minimum is −1, then k = −1, a>0, and from f(0)=4a−1=3 we get a=1. If the point is (1, 0), then a+k=0 and 4a+k=3, so a=1 and k=−1. On the other hand, with “opens upward” and “meets at two points,” a can take several values, and the point (4, 3) is information we already know.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.prompt: Build three different quadratic functions f(x) = ax² + bx + c with f(0) = 3 and f(4) = 3 whose graphs meet the x-axis at two different points. (Enter a, b, c.)
z-m-38-02.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute f(0)=3 and f(4)=3 into the formula, and first write down the relation between a and b.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.hint.1: Once you choose a, b is determined along with it. After choosing a, check whether the value of b²−4ac is positive.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.hint.2: Test negative values of a as well as positive ones.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a quadratic function (a is not 0).
z-m-38-02.s.s2.fail.c1: If a is 0, it is not a quadratic function.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Substituting x=0 gives f(0)=c, so c must be 3.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The value 16a+4b+c, obtained by substituting x=4, is not 3.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.ok.c4: It meets the x-axis at two different points (the discriminant is positive).
z-m-38-02.s.s2.fail.c4: The discriminant b²−4ac is not positive, so it does not meet the x-axis at two different points.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.explain: c = 3, and from 16a + 4b + 3 = 3 we get b = −4a. Then the discriminant is 16a² − 12a = 4a(4a − 3), which is positive when a < 0 or a > 3/4. So there are infinitely many formulas that satisfy all the conditions, such as (1, −4, 3), (2, −8, 3), (−1, 4, 3). a = 0.5 does not work because the discriminant is negative.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.prompt: In your own words, write why the formula is still not uniquely determined even when we add the information “meets the x-axis at two different points.”
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare what is different among the three formulas you built above.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Look at which of b and c changes along with it when you change a.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: Even if I change a, ...
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you show that the formulas you made are different, using specific values of a and b?
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the conditions keep being satisfied even when a changes (b is determined by a)?
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish “not determined” from “has no solution”?
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.model.0: The condition of meeting the x-axis at two points keeps being satisfied even if we change a to several values like 1, 2, −1 and set b to −4a, so there are several formulas that satisfy all the conditions. That is why it is not determined uniquely.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.model.1: Even with f(0)=3 and f(4)=3, the discriminant is positive both when a=1 and when a=2, so several different formulas come out. This condition does not fix the value of a.
z-m-38-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: It would be even better to also mention a case like a=−1, where the graph opens downward.

z-m-38-03.title: In Minjun's solution of √(x+2)=x, which line is wrong?
z-m-38-03.topic: Solutions of an irrational equation and extraneous solutions (conditions of irrational expressions)
z-m-38-03.goal: In a solution that squares both sides of an irrational equation, find the line where a check is missing, explain why one solution is discarded, and build an equation where the same thing happens.
z-m-38-03.material: x is a real number. Minjun solved the equation √(x+2) = x (read as: 'square root of x plus 2 equals x') and wrote the work below. The teacher said, “There may not be just one answer, so see whether any line of the solution lacks a check.”
z-m-38-03.thinking.0: Checking the logic of the solution line by line
z-m-38-03.thinking.1: Telling apart what the checking step should check
z-m-38-03.thinking.2: Designing a new problem with the same structure yourself
z-m-38-03.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty level assigned in production; it does not mean the curriculum places this content in high school grade 1. Assume the prerequisites below have already been learned.
z-m-38-03.prereq.1: Irrational expressions (the inside of a square root is 0 or more, and the value of a square root is 0 or more)
z-m-38-03.prereq.2: Solving a quadratic equation by factoring
z-m-38-03.prereq.3: Relations between roots and coefficients (sum and product of the two roots)
z-m-38-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line of the solution that contains something wrong. (Count the lines from 1.)
z-m-38-03.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute x = 2 and x = −1 each into the original equation √(x+2) = x, and calculate the left side and the right side separately.
z-m-38-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one how each line follows from the line right before it.
z-m-38-03.s.s1.line.0: Squaring both sides gives x + 2 = x²
z-m-38-03.s.s1.line.3: When x = −1, the inside of the root is −1 + 2 = 1, which is not negative, so both values are solutions of this equation
z-m-38-03.s.s1.explain: The 4th line is wrong. If you substitute x = −1 into the original equation, the left side is √1 = 1 and the right side is −1, so they differ. What needs to be checked is not whether “the inside of the root is not negative” but whether “the original equation holds.” The calculations in lines 1 to 3 are correct.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the correct explanations for why x = −1 is left out of the solutions.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.hint.0: First write the range of values that √(x+2) can take, and think about what condition that gives to x on the right side.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.hint.1: Apply the equation that gives x + 2 = x² in the same way to √(x+2) = −x.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.o.a: When squared, √(x+2)=x and √(x+2)=−x both become the same x+2=x², so they cannot be told apart
z-m-38-03.s.s2.r.a: This explanation recognizes that squaring erases information about the sign.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.o.b: After squaring there is always one more solution than in the original equation, so one of the solutions obtained by squaring must always be discarded
z-m-38-03.s.s2.r.b: Squaring does not always add one more solution. This generalizes without testing it yourself on an equation like √x = 2.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.o.c: There was a calculation mistake in the factoring (x−2)(x+1)=0 that created an extra solution
z-m-38-03.s.s2.r.c: The factoring is correct. This treats the fact that the quadratic equation has two solutions as a calculation mistake.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.o.d: It is enough that x+2 inside the root is not negative, so every solution with x ≥ −2 must be kept even if it came from squaring
z-m-38-03.s.s2.r.d: The condition inside the root is necessary but not sufficient. You have to check separately whether the original equation holds.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.o.e: √(x+2) is 0 or more, so x in the original equation must also be 0 or more, but the squared equation does not have this condition
z-m-38-03.s.s2.r.e: This explanation recognizes that the condition that a square root is 0 or more creates a condition on the right side as well.
z-m-38-03.s.s2.explain: a and e explain the same phenomenon from different sides. Squaring erases the sign information (a), so the condition 'x ≥ 0' that the original equation had disappears (e). b is a wrong generalization, c is wrong because the factoring is correct, and d is a necessary condition but does not tell you by itself whether a value is a solution.
z-m-38-03.s.s3.prompt: When a is a positive integer, squaring both sides of the equation √(x+a) = x gives x² − x − a = 0. Make three different values of a for which both roots of this quadratic equation are integers. (In that case, one of the two roots is not a solution of the original equation.)
z-m-38-03.s.s3.hint.0: Call the two roots r and s, and write how the sum r + s and the product rs are related to a.
z-m-38-03.s.s3.hint.1: Try small positive integers for a one at a time, test whether x² − x − a factors, and look for a pattern among the values of a that work.
z-m-38-03.s.s3.fail.c1: a must be an integer that is 1 or more.
z-m-38-03.s.s3.ok.c2: Both roots of x²−x−a=0 are integers (the discriminant 1+4a is a perfect square).
z-m-38-03.s.s3.fail.c2: The roots of x²−x−a=0 are not integers. Check whether the discriminant 1+4a is the square of some integer.
z-m-38-03.s.s3.explain: Call the two roots r and s. Then r + s = 1 and rs = −a < 0, so one root is positive and one is negative. The negative root cannot be a solution of the original equation because √(x+a) ≥ 0. For both roots to be integers, r(1−r) = −a, so a = r(r−1), and a = 2 (roots 2, −1), 6 (roots 3, −2), 12 (roots 4, −3), 20 (roots 5, −4), ...

z-m-38-04.title: If two formulas both fit all three records, which one should we trust?
z-m-38-04.topic: Choosing the formula that fits the data (comparing an inverse proportion and a quadratic function)
z-m-38-04.goal: Compare two kinds of formulas that pass through the same three data points, decide which formula to trust and how much using a new measurement and the structure of the situation, and state the range in which you trust it.
z-m-38-04.material: 12 L of water is poured equally into x identical bottles (x is a positive integer), and the amount y (L) in one bottle is measured. Records: with 1 bottle, 12 L; with 2 bottles, 6 L; with 3 bottles, 4 L. Two friends proposed formulas. Jiwon: y = 12/x (read as: '12 divided by x'). Hyunwoo: y = 2x² − 12x + 22 (read as: '2 x squared minus 12x plus 22'). The water does not leak, and it is divided equally among the bottles.
z-m-38-04.thinking.0: Calculating yourself to check whether the data and the model agree
z-m-38-04.thinking.1: Adjusting how strongly you believe something as new evidence arrives
z-m-38-04.thinking.2: Telling apart what fits the data from what fits the situation
z-m-38-04.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty level assigned in production; it does not mean the curriculum places this content in high school grade 1. Assume the prerequisites below have already been learned.
z-m-38-04.prereq.1: Finding function values (substituting x into the formula and calculating)
z-m-38-04.prereq.2: Reading the formulas of a quadratic function and of the rational function y=k/x
z-m-38-04.prereq.3: The relation (number of bottles) × (amount in one bottle) = total amount
z-m-38-04.s.s1.prompt: Looking at only the three records above, choose the most appropriate statement.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute x = 1, 2, 3 into each of the two formulas and compare with the records in a table.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the formula passing through three points is the only one, or whether there could be several.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.o.a: y=12/x is simpler, so these records alone are enough to conclude that Jiwon's formula is right
z-m-38-04.s.s1.r.a: You used “the formula is simple” as if it were evidence. Simplicity can be a reason to believe something, but it is not settled by the data.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.o.b: y=2x²−12x+22 has all integer coefficients and so is more accurate, so Hyunwoo's formula is right
z-m-38-04.s.s1.r.b: You looked for accuracy in the look of the coefficients. Whether a formula fits the data can only be known by substituting values.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.o.c: Both formulas fit the three records, so these records alone cannot tell which one is right
z-m-38-04.s.s1.r.c: This judgment recognizes that when two formulas fit the same data, the data alone cannot tell them apart.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.o.d: The formula through three points is unique, so one of the two must have a calculation mistake
z-m-38-04.s.s1.r.d: You believed that the formula through three points is unique. Even if a quadratic function passes through three points, a different kind of formula can pass through the same points.
z-m-38-04.s.s1.explain: Substituting x = 1, 2, 3 gives 12, 6, 4 for both formulas, which matches the records. Since two formulas fit the same data, the records alone cannot tell them apart. To decide which formula to trust, you need other grounds, such as a new measurement or the structure of the situation.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.prompt: New information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, decide how your belief in the two formulas changes.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute the revealed number of bottles x into both formulas to find the predicted values yourself, and compare them with the measured value.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.hint.1: When the measured value differs from the prediction, think about both possibilities: the formula may be wrong, or the measurement may be wrong.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.info: We divided the water among 4 bottles and measured the amount in one bottle: it was 3 L.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.ask: When you compare this measured value with the predictions of the two formulas, what do you conclude about the two formulas?
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.after: Jiwon's formula predicts 3 L at x = 4, and Hyunwoo's predicts 6 L. The measured 3 L agrees with Jiwon's formula and differs greatly from Hyunwoo's. It is reasonable to trust Jiwon's side right away, and it is also reasonable to measure once more because of the possibility of a measurement error.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.o.a: The measurement may be wrong, so measure once more and then decide
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.r.a: This is a careful attitude: not jumping to a conclusion from one measured value, but wanting to check.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.r.b: This judgment trusts more the one whose prediction differs less from the measured value.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.0.r.c: This judgment did not check what value Hyunwoo's formula gives at x = 4.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.info: With 6 bottles it measured 2 L, and with 12 bottles it measured 1 L. (So far, 5 records.)
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.ask: What is an appropriate way to state your belief in Jiwon's formula y = 12/x?
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.after: As the data grows, your belief in Jiwon's formula grows. But 5 records alone cannot guarantee every x. If there is a reason (the structure of the situation), your belief can be made firmer.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.o.a: All 5 records were right, so we can conclude that it is right for every positive integer x
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.r.a: You extended “the records were right five times” to all cases. The x values that were not measured have not been checked yet.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.o.b: Even if the number of records that fit increases, our belief does not change at all
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.r.b: This does not take into account that a new measurement is evidence pointing in the same direction.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.o.c: Our belief has grown because 5 records fit, but a separate reason is still needed for it to hold at the x values that were not measured
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.1.r.c: This judgment says that evidence strengthens belief, but a reason is needed to generalize to all cases.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.info: If you multiply the number of bottles by the amount in one bottle, you always get a total of 12 L. This is because the water does not leak and is divided equally among the bottles.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.ask: Knowing this, what can you say about Jiwon's formula y = 12/x?
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.after: Since x·y = 12, y = 12/x comes directly from the situation, not from the records. So we can say it holds for every positive integer x under the assumption that “the water does not leak and is divided equally.” If the assumption breaks (if water leaks), the formula changes too.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.o.a: Not only because of the records but because of the structure of the situation, we can say y=12/x for every positive integer x as long as the water does not leak and is divided equally
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.r.a: This judgment sets the range of belief using both reasons together: the evidence from the data and the structure of the situation.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.o.b: We still have to rely only on the 5 records, and the structure of the situation is not a ground
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.r.b: You missed that the relation that comes from the situation (the product is constant) directly determines the formula.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.o.c: Hyunwoo's formula happens to pass through the three points, so Jiwon's formula is wrong
z-m-38-04.s.s2.st.2.r.c: Hyunwoo's formula passing through the three points does not mean Jiwon's formula is wrong. His formula does not match the structure at other x values.
z-m-38-04.s.s2.reflect: At s1 you judged “we can't tell them apart,” and some people changed that after seeing the 4-bottle measurement, while others kept it with “measure once more.” Say whether the reason your judgment changed or stayed was the measured value or the structure of the situation.
z-m-38-04.s.s3.prompt: Hyunwoo said, “Still, the quadratic fit the three records, so it may be right later.” Explain the grounds for why Hyunwoo's formula does not fit this situation, using at least one number.
z-m-38-04.s.s3.hint.0: Substitute x = 4, 6, 10, and so on into Hyunwoo's formula to find the predicted values, and check whether they are possible values in the real situation.
z-m-38-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the amount in one bottle should change as the number of bottles grows, and how the value of the formula changes.
z-m-38-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When x = ..., Hyunwoo's formula gives ... L, but ...
z-m-38-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the number you gave a value you calculated by substituting it into Hyunwoo's formula?
z-m-38-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why that value does not fit the situation (if there are more bottles the amount should decrease, it cannot be larger than the total amount, and so on)?
z-m-38-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you understand and write why “it fit three points” is not enough as a ground?
z-m-38-04.s.s3.model.0: When x=4, Hyunwoo's formula gives 6 L, but we actually measured 3 L. Also, it does not fit the situation that the amount in one bottle gets larger again after the bottles increased. So even though it fits three points, we should not use this formula.
z-m-38-04.s.s3.model.1: If x=10, Hyunwoo's formula gives 2×100−120+22=102 L, which is more than the total 12 L of water. It fit the three records but is off at other values, so it cannot be trusted.
z-m-38-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer uses an impossible value in the situation as its ground, instead of the measured value.

z-m-38-05.title: If we multiply two increasing functions, is the product always increasing too?
z-m-38-05.topic: Increasing functions and products: building counterexamples from products of linear functions, and conditions under which the claim holds
z-m-38-05.goal: Test the claim “the product of two increasing functions is increasing,” build different counterexamples with linear functions, and choose the conditions under which the claim holds.
z-m-38-05.material: There are two functions f and g whose domain is all real numbers. “Increasing” means that if x₁ < x₂, then f(x₁) < f(x₂). Seoa said, “If f and g are both increasing functions, then the product h(x) = f(x)·g(x) is also an increasing function.” Seoa took f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x + 1 and calculated h at x = 1, 2, 3. h(1) = 6, h(2) = 15, h(3) = 28.
z-m-38-05.thinking.0: Testing a claim (not declaring it true from a few examples)
z-m-38-05.thinking.2: Using counterexamples to filter and choose the conditions under which it holds
z-m-38-05.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty level assigned in production; it does not mean the curriculum places this content in high school grade 1. Assume the prerequisites below have already been learned.
z-m-38-05.prereq.1: The meaning of a function being increasing (if x₁<x₂, then f(x₁)<f(x₂))
z-m-38-05.prereq.2: Calculating the values of linear functions and their product (x+m)(x+n)
z-m-38-05.prereq.3: The fact that a single counterexample is enough to show a claim is false
z-m-38-05.s.s1.prompt: Looking at Seoa's calculation, what is the most appropriate thing to say about Seoa's claim?
z-m-38-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write down the range of x that Seoa tested, and compare it with the whole domain.
z-m-38-05.s.s1.hint.1: For f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x + 1, also find the values of h when x is −3, −2, −1, 0.
z-m-38-05.s.s1.o.a: The values of h grew in order at x = 1, 2, 3, so we consider the claim true
z-m-38-05.s.s1.r.a: You extended the fact that three values grew to the whole domain. For a function to be increasing, it has to hold for all x₁<x₂.
z-m-38-05.s.s1.o.b: Since f and g are both increasing, it follows directly that the product is increasing, so no checking is needed
z-m-38-05.s.s1.r.b: You accepted the claim instead of treating it as something to check. Unlike a sum, a product is affected by signs.
z-m-38-05.s.s1.o.c: The tested x values are only positive, so it is hard to say it is true before seeing the values on the negative side too
z-m-38-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment separates the tested range from the whole domain and decides where to test further.
z-m-38-05.s.s1.o.d: Values grow fast, like h(3)=28, so we can regard the product as increasing
z-m-38-05.s.s1.r.d: You paid attention to how much the values grow. What the claim says is not about the size of the growth but about increasing at every x.
z-m-38-05.s.s1.explain: At x = −3, −2, −1, 0, h is 10, 3, 0, 1. Going from x = −3 to −2, h decreases from 10 to 3. Seoa's example tested only the positive side, so we could not tell whether the claim was true, and in fact the claim breaks even in this example.
z-m-38-05.s.s2.prompt: f(x) = x + m and g(x) = x + n (m ≤ n) are both increasing functions. Now build examples where the product h(x) = f(x)·g(x) is not increasing. That is, make h(p) > h(q) for some two numbers p < q. Make 3 examples with different (m, n).
z-m-38-05.s.s2.hint.0: After choosing m and n, make a table of the values of h(x) at x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1 and look for a place where the values decrease.
z-m-38-05.s.s2.hint.1: When you find a place where the values decrease, write those two x values as p and q. Change m and n and test whether other (m, n) also have a place where the values decrease.
z-m-38-05.s.s2.ok.c1: m is not greater than n (so that the same pair of functions is not counted twice with just the names swapped).
z-m-38-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make m ≤ n (so that the same example with f and g swapped is not counted twice).
z-m-38-05.s.s2.fail.c2: p must be less than q.
z-m-38-05.s.s2.ok.c3: p < q but h(p) > h(q). h is not increasing.
z-m-38-05.s.s2.fail.c3: h(p) is not greater than h(q). Calculate for yourself how the value of the product changes.
z-m-38-05.s.s2.explain: For example, if f(x) = g(x) = x (m = n = 0), then h(x) = x² and h(−2) = 4 > h(−1) = 1. If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x + 3 (m = 1, n = 3), then h(−3) = (−2)(0) = 0 > h(−2) = (−1)(1) = −1. One counterexample is enough to break the claim. Where the values of the two linear expressions are negative, the size of the product can get smaller as x increases.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.prompt: We want to add a condition so that Seoa's claim always holds. Which condition is appropriate?
z-m-38-05.s.s3.hint.0: For each condition, test whether you can build a pair of functions that satisfies the condition but whose product is not increasing.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.hint.1: To compare f(p)g(p) and f(q)g(q) when p < q, think about what sign the numbers multiplying f(p) < f(q) and g(p) < g(q) must have.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.o.a: The graphs of f and g both pass through the origin and rise toward the upper right
z-m-38-05.s.s3.r.a: f(x) = g(x) = x is an increasing function through the origin, but h(x) = x² decreases for x < 0. You did not build a counterexample to test it.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.o.b: The function values f(0) and g(0) at x = 0 are both positive
z-m-38-05.s.s3.r.b: You missed that it could be positive only at x = 0 and negative at other x. Test with f(x) = g(x) = x + 1 at x = −3, −2.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.o.c: Think of the domain as reduced to the part where x > 0
z-m-38-05.s.s3.r.c: Even if the domain is positive, the function values can be negative. Test with f(x) = g(x) = x − 5 at x = 1, 2.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.o.d: At every x in the domain, f(x) and g(x) are both positive
z-m-38-05.s.s3.r.d: This choice distinguishes the domain from the function values and recognizes that the signs of the numbers being multiplied matter when comparing products.
z-m-38-05.s.s3.explain: If p < q, then 0 < f(p) < f(q) and 0 < g(p) < g(q), so f(p)g(p) < f(q)g(p) < f(q)g(q). The counterexample for a is f = g = x (h is 4, 1 at x = −2, −1), the counterexample for b is f = g = x + 1 (h is 4, 1 at x = −3, −2), and the counterexample for c is f = g = x − 5 (h is 16, 9 at x = 1, 2).

z-m-38-06.title: When the domain and range are fixed, how many quadratic functions are possible?
z-m-38-06.topic: Determining the coefficients of a quadratic function whose domain and range are fixed
z-m-38-06.goal: Find as many as possible of the coefficients of f(x)=a(x−1)²+k whose range is 1 ≤ y ≤ 5 on the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, and explain why the cases split into two and why there are no more.
z-m-38-06.material: The quadratic function f(x) = a(x − 1)² + k (a ≠ 0; a and k are real constants; read as: 'a times (x minus 1) squared plus k') has domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and range 1 ≤ y ≤ 5. That is, on this interval the minimum is 1 and the maximum is 5. Note: at x = 0, x = 1, x = 3 in the domain, the function values are a + k, k, 4a + k, respectively. Minjun said, “There is a minimum, so it opens upward. So there is only one possible pair (a, k).”
z-m-38-06.thinking.0: Finding several solutions that satisfy the constraints
z-m-38-06.thinking.1: Dividing into cases and checking them without missing any
z-m-38-06.thinking.2: Writing the reason for the claim that there are no more
z-m-38-06.prereq.0: The H1 of this task is only a difficulty level assigned in production; it does not mean the curriculum places this content in high school grade 1. Assume the prerequisites below have already been learned.
z-m-38-06.prereq.1: The sign of a and the shape of the graph for the quadratic y=a(x−p)²+q
z-m-38-06.prereq.2: On a closed interval, the maximum and minimum come from among the values at the vertex and the two endpoints
z-m-38-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most appropriate judgment about Minjun's statement.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write where the largest value and the smallest value on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 occur when a is positive and when a is negative.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a graph with a negative, and check whether the vertex is the highest or the lowest point of the interval.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.o.a: No. Even if it opens downward, the minimum 1 can occur at an endpoint, so there can be another pair
z-m-38-06.s.s1.r.a: This judgment recognizes that when the interval is closed, the minimum can occur at an endpoint other than the vertex.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.o.b: Right. The range has a minimum, so it opens upward, and then there is only one pair (a, k)
z-m-38-06.s.s1.r.b: You missed that a closed interval always has a minimum. The fact that a minimum exists does not decide the sign of a.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.o.c: No. Whether a is positive or negative, there are infinitely many consecutive values, so there are infinitely many possible pairs
z-m-38-06.s.s1.r.c: You missed that two conditions (minimum and maximum) determine two unknowns. You did not set up equations and solve.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.o.d: Right. The vertex is inside the interval, so k is determined as the minimum 1, and the rest is also determined uniquely, so that is all
z-m-38-06.s.s1.r.d: You considered only the case where a is positive. If a is negative, the value k at the vertex becomes the maximum.
z-m-38-06.s.s1.explain: The vertex x = 1 lies inside the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 3. If a > 0, the minimum is k and the maximum is the value 4a + k at the endpoint x = 3. If a < 0, the maximum is k and the minimum is the value 4a + k at the endpoint x = 3. You have to solve the two cases separately.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter as many pairs (a, k) as you can for which the range on the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 is 1 ≤ y ≤ 5. You need at least two different pairs. (We won't tell you the maximum number of pairs.)
z-m-38-06.s.s2.hint.0: Assume a is positive, decide which of the values at x = 0, 1, 3 is the smallest and which is the largest, and set up two equations.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.hint.1: Assume a is negative and do the same thing.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a quadratic function (a is not 0).
z-m-38-06.s.s2.fail.c1: If a is 0, it is not a quadratic function.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The maximum on the interval is 5.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The maximum on the interval is not 5. Check the largest among the values a+k, k, 4a+k at x=0, 1, 3.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The minimum on the interval is 1.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The minimum on the interval is not 1. Check the smallest among a+k, k, 4a+k.
z-m-38-06.s.s2.explain: If a > 0, the minimum is k = 1 and the maximum is 4a + 1 = 5, so a = 1. If a < 0, the maximum is k = 5 and the minimum is 4a + 5 = 1, so a = −1. So the only possible pairs are (1, 1) and (−1, 5).
z-m-38-06.s.s3.prompt: In your own words, write why you can be sure that there are no more possible (a, k) besides the pairs found above. You may also write where Minjun's statement fell short.
z-m-38-06.s.s3.hint.0: Count how many cases there are in all when you divide by the sign of a, and write where the minimum and the maximum occur in each case.
z-m-38-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how many of a or k are determined in each case.
z-m-38-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If a is positive, ...; if negative, ...
z-m-38-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you cover both cases divided by the sign of a?
z-m-38-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In each case, did you say whether the minimum and maximum come from the vertex or an endpoint?
z-m-38-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write that the reason for “no more” is that in each case only one a and one k are determined?
z-m-38-06.s.s3.model.0: If a is positive, it opens upward, so the minimum is k=1 at the vertex and the maximum is 4a+1=5 at the endpoint x=3, so a=1. If a is negative, it opens downward, so the maximum is k=5 and the minimum is 4a+5=1, so a=−1. There are only these two signs and one pair for each, so there are only two pairs.
z-m-38-06.s.s3.model.1: The vertex is inside the interval, so either the minimum or the maximum must be k. If it opens downward, k=5; if it opens upward, k=1. The other is determined by the value at the endpoint x=3, so only one a comes out in each case.
z-m-38-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: Without dividing by the sign first, I explained by dividing into the case where k is the maximum and the case where k is the minimum.
